q: The upper stretch of the river toward Luxembourg sits on limestone rather than slate and grows an ancient, ferociously tart white grape. Which?
exp: Elbling is one of the oldest varieties still worked in Germany and gives a thin, high-acid wine that mostly ends up as Sekt. The Obermosel's Muschelkalk is a completely different geology from the Devonian slate downstream.

q: A grower on one Mosel tributary loses whole vintages to unripeness in poor years yet makes the most piercing wine of the valley in good ones. Which tributary, and why?
opts: The Ruwer, because its soils are pure sand and hold no water
The Ruwer, because it lies south of the main valley and ripens too fast
The Saar, because it is colder and ripeness is not assured
The Saar, because it is planted mainly to red varieties
exp: The Saar is a side valley open to cold air, so the margin between ripe and unripe is thinner there than anywhere on the Mosel. When the year does deliver, the acidity gives wines of extraordinary tension and life.

q: A vineyard on a Mosel bend near Bremm is routinely called the steepest in Europe. Roughly what gradient does it reach?
exp: The Calmont is worked on ropes and a via ferrata runs through it for walkers. Anything approaching that angle can only be tended by hand, one vine at a time.

q: A guest asks for the lightest serious white on the list to drink with a lightly spiced dish. Which German bottling answers that best?
exp: Kabinett from the Mosel is usually the lowest in alcohol of anything worth cellaring, and its trace of sugar handles chilli and ginger that a dry wine would fight. The other three are all dry and considerably fuller.

q: For some thirty kilometres west of Wiesbaden the Rhine abandons its northward course and runs east to west. What does that hand the growers on its north bank?
opts: Shelter from the sun through the hottest part of the day
A northerly exposure that preserves acidity
A full southern exposure across a long stretch of slope
exp: The river turns west at Wiesbaden, runs to Rudesheim and turns north again at Bingen. The whole north bank therefore looks south across the water, and that sentence is most of what the Rheingau is.

q: A courier carrying harvest permission from the Prince-Abbot of Fulda arrived late in 1775, and the shrivelled, rotten grapes were picked and pressed anyway. Which estate tells that story?
exp: The wine turned out to be a revelation and Spatlese entered the language. The tale has been polished over two centuries, but the estate's records do show a late-picked wine from that harvest.

q: Riesling covers most of the Rheingau, but one village at its western end has grown red wine on slate for centuries. Which grape?
exp: Assmannshausen sits where the Rhine turns north into its gorge and the soils change from quartzite and loess to slate. Its Spatburgunder is pale, savoury and quite unlike the riper Baden style.

q: The English word hock, used for a century to mean Rhine wine of any kind, is a worn-down version of which Rheingau town's name?
exp: Hochheim sits apart from the rest of the Rheingau, on the river Main east of Wiesbaden. Queen Victoria's fondness for its wine did the rest, and the shortened name spread to cover everything German and white.

q: Volcanic porphyry, slate, quartzite, sandstone and loam all surface within a few kilometres of one river valley south-west of Bingen. Which region?
exp: The Nahe cuts through an unusually broken piece of geology, which is why no two of its villages taste alike. Its Rieslings are conventionally placed between the Mosel's delicacy and the Rheingau's weight.

q: One Nahe vineyard was terraced early in the twentieth century on the spoil of a worked-out copper mine and is now among the region's most celebrated. Which?
exp: Kupfergrube simply means copper mine, and the terraces were cut into volcanic rock left behind by the workings. The wines have a smoky, mineral cast that has nothing to do with the vine.

q: A steep, crumbling cliff of iron-stained red slate and sandstone drops straight to the Rhine at Nierstein and Nackenheim. What is that slope called?
exp: Rotliegend is the formation and Roter Hang, the red slope, is the name growers use. It carries Rheinhessen's finest Riesling sites, and almost all the rest of the region is far gentler ground.

q: Westhofen and Dalsheim sit inland from the Rhine in southern Rheinhessen, in a district that became the centre of the region's dry-wine revival. Which district?
exp: Wonnegau means something close to the district of delight. Its limestone and clay gave a generation of younger growers the raw material for serious dry Riesling after decades of anonymous blending.

q: Fig and almond trees grow among the vines along one German region's wine road, which is not what fifty degrees north would suggest. What makes that possible?
opts: The Rhine is at its widest here and stores enough heat to warm the air
Hills to the west shelter the vineyards and cast a rain shadow over them
The soils are volcanic and radiate warmth through the night
The vineyards sit high enough to stand above the frost line
exp: The Haardt is the northern continuation of the Vosges and wrings the rain out of the westerlies before they arrive. The Pfalz is one of the driest and warmest corners of Germany as a result.

q: Growers in one Mittelhaardt village have carted crushed black volcanic rock onto their vineyards for generations. Which village, and to what end?
opts: Wachenheim, because the stone smothers weeds between the rows
Ruppertsberg, because the stone opens up drainage in heavy clay
Forst, because the dark stone absorbs heat and warms sandy soil
Deidesheim, because the stone raises the acidity of the soil
exp: Basalt was quarried from an outcrop above the village and spread across the vineyards below. Kirchenstuck, Jesuitengarten and Pechstein are the sites that made the practice famous.

q: Two Bereiche divide the Pfalz along its length, one around Bad Durkheim and Forst and one running south toward the French border. What is the northern of the two generally called?
exp: The Mittelhaardt holds the classic Riesling villages of Forst, Deidesheim, Ruppertsberg and Wachenheim. The Sudliche Weinstrasse to the south is warmer again, and leans toward the Pinot family and Dornfelder.

q: A generation of growers took over family estates west of the Rhine from the 1990s and pulled a region famous for cheap semi-sweet blends round to dry, single-site Riesling. Which region?
exp: Rheinhessen carries more vineyard than any other German region, and for decades most of it went into Liebfraumilch. Lower yields, later picking and village and vineyard names on the label reversed that.
